about.title: Newport Beach Wrongful Death Claims
about.longDescription: Losing someone suddenly leaves a family sorting through grief and paperwork at the same time. In Newport Beach, the roads involved are often ones families drive every day. Public records for 2025 show 419 injury collisions across the city, 583 people hurt, and 2 traffic deaths, with Jamboree Road, MacArthur Boulevard and the SR-1 stretch of West Coast Highway carrying the largest share of reported collisions. A wrongful death claim is a civil action, separate from any criminal case. California limits who can bring it: a surviving spouse or domestic partner and children come first, followed by certain dependents and heirs. The deadline is generally two years from the date of death, and shorter when a government entity is involved. Recoverable losses include funeral and burial costs, the financial support your loved one would have provided, and the loss of their love, companionship and guidance. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm; the independent attorneys we connect Newport Beach families with work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: Is a wrongful death claim the same as the criminal case against the driver?
items.answer: No. A wrongful death claim is a civil action brought by the family, while a criminal case is brought by prosecutors. The two proceed on separate tracks, and a civil claim can move forward whether or not criminal charges are filed.

items.question: Our loved one was killed in a crash on West Coast Highway. Does the location change anything?
items.answer: It can. SR-1 runs through Newport Beach but is part of the state highway system, so if roadway design or maintenance is a factor, a public entity may be involved and the filing deadline becomes much shorter than two years. An attorney can sort out which parties and timelines apply.

items.question: What losses can our family actually recover?
items.answer: California allows recovery of funeral and burial costs, the financial support the person would have contributed over their lifetime, and the loss of love, companionship and guidance. Every family's situation is different, and no outcome can be promised. An attorney will review your circumstances and explain what is realistic.
